Lecture 5

Graphical Methods: Inequalities, Equations and Construction

Day 5 homework
On this page5.1 Constructing a Graph from Its Definition5.2 Reading a trigonometric inequality from a graph5.3 What a graph can suggest, and what a proof must establish5.4 Solving equations graphically: pictures, comparisons and root counts5.5 Chords of the sine curve and inequalities between slopes5.6 Choosing a Graphical Method5.7 Further Study after Calculus

In Lecture 4 we learnt to recognise symmetry, repetition and the direction in which a graph moves. We now use those observations to answer questions. Where is one curve above another? How many intersections are possible? How can we construct a curve whose formula changes from one interval to the next?

A drawing is a guide to a proof, not a substitute for one. A crossing may lie outside the displayed window. Two curves may touch without crossing. A jump may change an inequality from false to true without passing through equality. This lecture develops a method for each of these situations.

§ Reading route and conventions

All variables are real unless stated otherwise, and all angles are measured in radians. We first review graph construction, then solve trigonometric inequalities, read and check intersection counts, and study greatest-integer graphs. The final numbered section contains Homework of Day 5; its complete solutions are in Solutions of Day 5.

For the first reading, use the tools already developed in this module: domain restrictions, range, symmetry, increasing and decreasing functions, periodicity, and the trigonometric identities. The parent-graph atlas is available whenever a familiar curve needs to be recalled.

At a few points we read a feature of a familiar curve: an unbroken branch crosses a line, or an arch lies above a chord. We shall explain these pictures in ordinary language. Their full justification uses ideas such as continuity, which belong to the next Calculus module and are not assumed here. The section Further Study after Calculus supplies those later arguments, including derivative methods. Leave it until after that module. On a first reading, go from the graphical review directly to Homework of Day 5.

5.1 Constructing a Graph from Its Definition

One point at a time, then one interval at a time

Recall the graph of a function: it is the collection of points (x,f(x))(x,f(x)) for inputs in its domain. This definition tells us how to handle a piecewise formula. First select an input interval. Use only the formula assigned to that interval, and then stop the curve at its stated boundary. A formula in another part of the definition does not apply to this input.

An open circle at (a,b)(a,b) says that this particular point is excluded. It does not automatically mean that aa is excluded from the whole domain: another branch may contain (a,c)(a,c). A filled point at (a,c)(a,c) records the actual value f(a)=cf(a)=c. The vertical-line test still applies to the complete graph, not merely to each branch separately.

💡 A five-part graph specification

For each piece, record (1) its input interval; (2) its formula; (3) its intercepts or convenient exact points; (4) its open and closed endpoints; and (5) how the output changes as the input increases. After assembling the pieces, state the domain and read the range by projecting onto the vertical axis. These checks are used for every construction in Day 5 homework.

Transformations are rules for moving points

Suppose (u,v)(u,v) is on the graph of y=f(x)y=f(x), so v=f(u)v=f(u). The following table is obtained by substituting the new coordinates into the new formula. It therefore explains the transformations, rather than asking us to memorise which sign means which direction.

New functionPoint obtained from (u,v)(u,v)Interpretation
f(x)+kf(x)+k(u,v+k)(u,v+k)Add kk to every output; shift vertically.
f(x−h)f(x-h)(u+h,v)(u+h,v)To keep the old input uu, solve x−h=ux-h=u.
−f(x)-f(x)(u,−v)(u,-v)Reflect across the horizontal axis.
f(−x)f(-x)(−u,v)(-u,v)Reflect across the vertical axis.
cf(x)c f(x), c≠0c\ne0(u,cv)(u,cv)Multiply vertical coordinates by cc.
f(bx)f(bx), b≠0b\ne0(u/b,v)(u/b,v)Divide horizontal coordinates by bb.

The domain moves with the horizontal coordinates. For example, if ff is defined only for u≥0u\ge0, then f(x−h)f(x-h) is defined only when x−h≥0x-h\ge0, or x≥hx\ge h. A transformation changes points and restrictions together.

Example 5.1

A point-based transformation

Construct y=(x−2)2−1y=(x-2)^2-1 from y=x2y=x^2.

Solution.

Write u=x−2u=x-2, so x=u+2x=u+2. If the original point is (u,u2)(u,u^2), the new point is (u+2,u2−1)(u+2,u^2-1). Thus we shift two units right and one unit down. The vertex (0,0)(0,0) becomes (2,−1)(2,-1). The points (−1,1)(-1,1) and (1,1)(1,1) become (1,0)(1,0) and (3,0)(3,0). Both graphs have domain ℝ\mathbb{R}; the original range [0,∞)[0,\infty) becomes [−1,∞)[-1,\infty).

The dashed arrow connects the old vertex with its image. It is a point movement, not an extra branch of either function.

Comparing graphs means comparing their heights

At a fixed input xx, the number f(x)−g(x)f(x)-g(x) is the signed vertical separation of the graphs. Consequently, f(x)>g(x)⇔f(x)−g(x)>0,f(x)=g(x)⇔f(x)−g(x)=0.f(x)>g(x)\iff f(x)-g(x)>0, \qquad f(x)=g(x)\iff f(x)-g(x)=0. Only inputs in the common domain are eligible. We will repeatedly use this translation: draw two curves to see the situation, and study their difference to justify the answer. For graphs with separate pieces or jumps, also examine each jump and its actual endpoint value.

5.2 Reading a trigonometric inequality from a graph

An equation such as sinx=−1/2\sin x=-1/2 asks where two graphs meet. An inequality such as sinx>−1/2\sin x>-1/2 asks on which side of those intersection points one graph lies above the other. The answer is usually an interval of inputs, not a finite list of angles.

In this lecture all angles are measured in radians. Unless an interval is specified, solving an inequality means finding every real input in its domain that makes it true. A sketch helps us find the answer; exact values, monotonicity and endpoint checks justify the answer.

💡 A reliable five-step method

  1. Write the domain before simplifying. A point at which the original expression is undefined can never become a solution.

  2. Choose one interval covering a complete period. For sine and cosine the period is 2π2\pi; for tangent it is π\pi.

  3. Find the intersections with the comparison line exactly.

  4. Use the graph and monotonicity between consecutive intersections to select the required intervals. Include an endpoint only when the original expression is defined there and the inequality permits equality.

  5. Translate the selected intervals by every integer multiple of the period, and undo any substitution carefully.

The background ideas are reviewed in Lecture 4: monotonicity and Lecture 4: periodic functions. If FF has period T>0T>0, then F(x+nT)=F(x)F(x+nT)=F(x) for every integer nn for which the expressions are defined. Consequently, an inequality F(x)>cF(x)>c has the same truth value at xx and at x+nTx+nT. The translated intervals describe the entire solution because every real number can be moved into a chosen period interval by subtracting an integer multiple of TT.

Read the interval notation aloud. The interval (a,b)(a,b) means a<x<ba<x<b, whereas [a,b)[a,b) means a≤x<ba\le x<b. The symbol ⋃n∈ℤIn\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}I_n means “take every point belonging to at least one of the intervals InI_n.” It is the natural notation for a repeating family of solution intervals.

Example 5.2

Above a negative level

Solve sinx>−1/2\sin x>-1/2.

Solution.

The domain of sine is ℝ\mathbb{R}, and its period is 2π2\pi. Choose the period interval [−π/2,3π/2][-\pi/2,3\pi/2]. The endpoints represent the same height, so there is no harm in drawing both of them; the final answer will be a union of translated intervals.

The comparison line is y=−1/2y=-1/2. Its intersections with sine in this period occur at x=−π6andx=7π6,x=-\frac\pi6\qquad\text{and}\qquad x=\frac{7\pi}6, because sin(−π/6)=−1/2\sin(-\pi/6)=-1/2 and sin(7π/6)=−sin(π/6)=−1/2\sin(7\pi/6)=-\sin(\pi/6)=-1/2. By the sine graph, sine rises from −1-1 to 11 on [−π/2,π/2][-\pi/2,\pi/2], and then falls from 11 to −1-1 on [π/2,3π/2][\pi/2,3\pi/2]. It is therefore above the line precisely between the two intersections: −π6<x<7π6.-\frac\pi6<x<\frac{7\pi}6. Neither endpoint is allowed: at either one, the two sides of the original strict inequality are equal. Repeating with period 2π2\pi gives x∈⋃n∈ℤ(2nπ−π6,2nπ+7π6).\boxed{x\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} \left(2n\pi-\frac\pi6,\,2n\pi+\frac{7\pi}6\right).} For example, x=0x=0 belongs to the interval with n=0n=0, and indeed sin0=0>−1/2\sin0=0>-1/2. The point x=3π/2x=3\pi/2 does not belong to any of the intervals, and sin(3π/2)=−1\sin(3\pi/2)=-1 fails the inequality.

Example 5.3

Below a level, including equality

Solve cosx≤−1/2\cos x\le-1/2.

Solution.

The domain is ℝ\mathbb{R}, and the period is 2π2\pi. On [0,2π][0,2\pi], the equation cosx=−1/2\cos x=-1/2 has the two solutions x=2π3andx=4π3.x=\frac{2\pi}3\quad\text{and}\quad x=\frac{4\pi}3. Cosine decreases on [0,π][0,\pi] and increases on [π,2π][\pi,2\pi]. It reaches the comparison line at 2π/32\pi/3, stays below it, and returns to it at 4π/34\pi/3. Thus the part of this period satisfying the inequality is [2π/3,4π/3][2\pi/3,4\pi/3].

This time both endpoints are included because the symbol is ≤\le, and cosine is defined at both endpoints. Therefore x∈⋃n∈ℤ[2nπ+2π3,2nπ+4π3].\boxed{x\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} \left[2n\pi+\frac{2\pi}3,\,2n\pi+\frac{4\pi}3\right].} At the middle point x=πx=\pi, the value is −1-1, which is below −1/2-1/2; at x=0x=0, the value is 11, which is not.

Example 5.4

Tangent and its shorter period

Solve tanx<2\tan x<2.

Solution.

First exclude the vertical asymptotes: x≠π2+nπ(n∈ℤ).x\ne\frac\pi2+n\pi\qquad(n\in\mathbb{Z}). Tangent is strictly increasing on its principal branch (−π/2,π/2)(-\pi/2,\pi/2). Let α=arctan2\alpha=\arctan2. By the definition of the principal inverse, −π/2<α<π/2-\pi/2<\alpha<\pi/2 and tanα=2\tan\alpha=2. In fact, π/4<α<π/2\pi/4<\alpha<\pi/2, since tan(π/4)=1<2\tan(\pi/4)=1<2. Strict increase gives the exact equivalence tanx<2⇔−π2<x<αon this branch.\tan x<2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -\frac\pi2<x<\alpha \qquad\text{on this branch}. The left endpoint is absent because tangent is undefined there; the right endpoint is absent because the inequality is strict. The period is π\pi, so the complete answer is x∈⋃n∈ℤ(nπ−π2,nπ+arctan2).\boxed{x\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} \left(n\pi-\frac\pi2,\,n\pi+\arctan2\right).} Why the period matters. Translating by 2nπ2n\pi would omit every other tangent branch. For example, x=πx=\pi satisfies tanπ=0<2\tan\pi=0<2, but it is missed by that incomplete family. The translation here must be by nπn\pi. Also, the familiar point on this graph is (π/4,1)(\pi/4,1), with input first and output second.

Example 5.5

Solve for the angle, then the input

Solve sin(3x2+π12)<12.\sin\left(\frac{3x}{2}+\frac\pi{12}\right)<\frac1{\sqrt2}.

Solution.

The expression is defined for every real xx. Introduce a new angle t=3x2+π12.t=\frac{3x}{2}+\frac\pi{12}. The inequality becomes sint<1/2\sin t<1/\sqrt2. The sine curve meets this level at t=π/4t=\pi/4 and t=3π/4t=3\pi/4 in [0,2π][0,2\pi]. It lies below the level from 3π/43\pi/4 up to the next occurrence of π/4\pi/4, which is 2π+π/4=9π/42\pi+\pi/4=9\pi/4. Thus a convenient single family, without splitting at 00, is 2nπ+3π4<t<2nπ+9π4,n∈ℤ.2n\pi+\frac{3\pi}4<t<2n\pi+\frac{9\pi}4, \qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}. Substitute the original angle back into this inequality: 2nπ+3π4<3x2+π12<2nπ+9π4,2nπ+9π−π12<3x2<2nπ+27π−π12,2nπ+2π3<3x2<2nπ+13π6,4nπ3+4π9<x<4nπ3+13π9.\begin{aligned} 2n\pi+\frac{3\pi}4 &<\frac{3x}{2}+\frac\pi{12} <2n\pi+\frac{9\pi}4,\\ 2n\pi+\frac{9\pi-\pi}{12} &<\frac{3x}{2} <2n\pi+\frac{27\pi-\pi}{12},\\ 2n\pi+\frac{2\pi}3 &<\frac{3x}{2} <2n\pi+\frac{13\pi}6,\\ \frac{4n\pi}3+\frac{4\pi}9 &<x<\frac{4n\pi}3+\frac{13\pi}9. \end{aligned} The last line follows by multiplying all three parts by the positive number 2/32/3, so neither inequality sign reverses. Hence x∈⋃n∈ℤ(4nπ3+4π9,4nπ3+13π9).\boxed{x\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} \left(\frac{4n\pi}3+\frac{4\pi}9, \frac{4n\pi}3+\frac{13\pi}9\right).} The translation length 4π/34\pi/3 is a useful check: increasing xx by 4π/34\pi/3 increases the angle 3x/2+π/123x/2+\pi/12 by exactly 2π2\pi.

Example 5.6

Combine sine and cosine first

Solve cos2x−sin2x≥0\cos2x-\sin2x\ge0.

Solution.

The addition formula says cos(u+v)=cosucosv−sinusinv\cos(u+v)=\cos u\cos v-\sin u\sin v. Since both cos(π/4)\cos(\pi/4) and sin(π/4)\sin(\pi/4) equal 1/21/\sqrt2, it gives cos2x−sin2x=2(12cos2x−12sin2x)=2cos(2x+π4).\begin{aligned} \cos2x-\sin2x &=\sqrt2\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\cos2x- \frac1{\sqrt2}\sin2x\right)\\ &=\sqrt2\cos\left(2x+\frac\pi4\right). \end{aligned} Dividing by 2>0\sqrt2>0 preserves the sign. If t=2x+π/4t=2x+\pi/4, our question is now cost≥0\cos t\ge0. Cosine is nonnegative precisely on the intervals 2nπ−π2≤t≤2nπ+π2,n∈ℤ.2n\pi-\frac\pi2\le t\le2n\pi+\frac\pi2, \qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}. Undo the substitution, one operation at a time: 2nπ−π2≤2x+π4≤2nπ+π2,2nπ−3π4≤2x≤2nπ+π4,nπ−3π8≤x≤nπ+π8.\begin{aligned} 2n\pi-\frac\pi2 &\le2x+\frac\pi4\le2n\pi+\frac\pi2,\\ 2n\pi-\frac{3\pi}4 &\le2x\le2n\pi+\frac\pi4,\\ n\pi-\frac{3\pi}8 &\le x\le n\pi+\frac\pi8. \end{aligned} Thus x∈⋃n∈ℤ[nπ−3π8,nπ+π8].\boxed{x\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} \left[n\pi-\frac{3\pi}8,\,n\pi+\frac\pi8\right].} There are no excluded points in the original domain, and both endpoints make the original difference zero. They must therefore be included. Notation check. The substituted angle is t=2x+π/4t=2x+\pi/4, not 2n+π/42n+\pi/4: xx is the input being solved for; nn indexes the repeated intervals.

5.3 What a graph can suggest, and what a proof must establish

A graph can suggest an inequality about three angles. But an attractive picture is not automatically a proof for all possible angles. We must check where the angles lie, how the curve bends on that interval, and when equality can occur.

Concavity and convexity. These are names for two pictures: a curve above its joining segments, or a curve below them. Naming the shape does not prove that a particular curve has it. We use the pictures to understand the next inequalities, and give algebraic calculations to establish those inequalities. To test the picture, pick two points on the curve, join them, and compare the curve and the segment at the same intermediate input.

A graph is concave on an interval if every line segment joining two points on it lies on or below the graph. It is convex if every such segment lies on or above the graph. The joining line segment is called a chord. With 0≤λ≤10\le\lambda\le1, these statements mean concave:f((1−λ)u+λv)≥(1−λ)f(u)+λf(v),convex:f((1−λ)u+λv)≤(1−λ)f(u)+λf(v).\begin{array}{ll} \text{concave:}& f((1-\lambda)u+\lambda v) \ge(1-\lambda)f(u)+\lambda f(v),\\[2pt] \text{convex:}& f((1-\lambda)u+\lambda v) \le(1-\lambda)f(u)+\lambda f(v). \end{array} The expression (1−λ)u+λv(1-\lambda)u+\lambda v is an input between uu and vv. The expression on the right is the height of the chord at that input. In the strict forms, the relevant inequality is strict when u≠vu\ne v and 0<λ<10<\lambda<1.

A centroid is an average of coordinates. If three plotted points have coordinates (A,f(A))(A,f(A)), (B,f(B))(B,f(B)), and (C,f(C))(C,f(C)), their centroid is G=(A+B+C3,f(A)+f(B)+f(C)3).G=\left(\frac{A+B+C}{3}, \frac{f(A)+f(B)+f(C)}{3}\right). Thus a comparison between the height of GG and the height of the curve at (A+B+C)/3(A+B+C)/3 is a comparison between an average of outputs and the output at an average input. These are generally different. The next two examples give algebraic proofs as well as the graphical interpretation, so their conclusions do not rest on the appearance of a single drawing.

Example 5.7

A cosine bound for a triangle

Let A,B,CA,B,C be the angles of a nondegenerate triangle; that is, A,B,C>0A,B,C>0 and A+B+C=πA+B+C=\pi. Prove cosA+cosB+cosC≤32.\cos A+\cos B+\cos C\le\frac32. Determine when equality holds, and hence state the strict version.

Solution.

Because all three angles are positive and sum to π\pi, each is less than π\pi. In particular, 0<C/2<π/20<C/2<\pi/2. Set s=sinC2,d=A−B2.s=\sin\frac C2,\qquad d=\frac{A-B}{2}. Then s>0s>0. The sum-to-product formula and A+B=π−CA+B=\pi-C give cosA+cosB=2cosA+B2cosA−B2=2cos(π2−C2)cosd=2scosd.\begin{aligned} \cos A+\cos B &=2\cos\frac{A+B}{2}\cos\frac{A-B}{2}\\ &=2\cos\left(\frac\pi2-\frac C2\right)\cos d\\ &=2s\cos d. \end{aligned} Also, cosC=1−2sin2(C/2)=1−2s2\cos C=1-2\sin^2(C/2)=1-2s^2. Therefore cosA+cosB+cosC=2scosd+1−2s2≤2s+1−2s2since s>0 and cosd≤1=32−2(s−12)2≤32since a square is nonnegative.\begin{aligned} \cos A+\cos B+\cos C &=2s\cos d+1-2s^2\\ &\le2s+1-2s^2 &&\text{since \(s>0\) and \(\cos d\le1\)}\\ &=\frac32-2\left(s-\frac12\right)^2\\ &\le\frac32 &&\text{since a square is nonnegative}. \end{aligned} This proves the inequality even when the triangle is obtuse.

For equality, both inequalities in the chain must be equalities. First, s=1/2s=1/2. By monotonicity, sine is strictly increasing on (0,π/2)(0,\pi/2). Hence sin(C/2)=1/2\sin(C/2)=1/2 implies C/2=π/6C/2=\pi/6, so C=π/3C=\pi/3. Second, cosd=1\cos d=1. Because −π/2<d<π/2-\pi/2<d<\pi/2, the only possibility is d=0d=0, so A=BA=B. Finally, A+B=π−C=2π3⇒A=B=π3.A+B=\pi-C=\frac{2\pi}3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A=B=\frac\pi3. Conversely, the equilateral triangle has three cosines equal to 1/21/2, so its sum really is 3/23/2. We have proved cosA+cosB+cosC≤32,with equality exactly when A=B=C=π/3.\boxed{\cos A+\cos B+\cos C\le\frac32, \quad\text{with equality exactly when }A=B=C=\pi/3.} The inequality is strict for every non-equilateral triangle. Pairwise distinctness is stronger than necessary; “not all equal” suffices.

Why the angle restrictions matter. Distinct real angles need not have distinct cosines. For example, A=−5π3,B=π3,C=7π3A=-\frac{5\pi}3,\quad B=\frac\pi3,\quad C=\frac{7\pi}3 are pairwise distinct, have sum π\pi, and each has cosine 1/21/2. Thus the condition A+B+C=πA+B+C=\pi, even together with pairwise distinctness, does not make the inequality strict for arbitrary real angles. Restricting the angles to those of a triangle allows us to identify equality with the equilateral case.

What remains true for unrestricted real angles? The non-strict bound cosA+cosB+cosC≤3/2\cos A+\cos B+\cos C\le3/2 still holds whenever A+B+C=πA+B+C=\pi, even without positivity. To see this, set p=(A+B)/2p=(A+B)/2, q=(A−B)/2q=(A-B)/2, and r=|cosp|r=|\cos p|. Then 0≤r≤10\le r\le1, and cosA+cosB+cosC=2cospcosq−cos(2p)=1+2cospcosq−2cos2p≤1+2|cosp|−2cos2p=32−2(r−12)2≤32.\begin{aligned} \cos A+\cos B+\cos C &=2\cos p\cos q-\cos(2p)\\ &=1+2\cos p\cos q-2\cos^2p\\ &\le1+2|\cos p|-2\cos^2p\\ &=\frac32-2\left(r-\frac12\right)^2\le\frac32. \end{aligned} Thus positivity is not needed for the non-strict bound. Without positivity, however, distinct angles can still give equality because cosine is periodic.

Why not apply the same picture blindly to an obtuse triangle? Cosine is concave on [0,π/2][0,\pi/2], but its bending changes after π/2\pi/2. An obtuse angle lies outside that concavity interval. Thus a single concavity argument on the entire interval [0,π][0,\pi] is invalid. The proof above does not make that assumption: it uses only a sum-to-product identity, cosd≤1\cos d\le1, and a nonnegative square.

Example 5.8

An algebraic reduction to tangent

Solve sinxcosx+12tanx≥1.\sin x\cos x+\frac12\tan x\ge1.

Solution.

Because tangent occurs, the original domain excludes x=π/2+nπx=\pi/2+n\pi, n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. On this domain set y=tanxy=\tan x. Then sinxcosx=sinxcosxcos2x=tanx11+tan2x=y1+y2.\sin x\cos x =\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\cos^2x =\tan x\,\frac1{1+\tan^2x} =\frac{y}{1+y^2}. Here we used the trigonometric identities 1+tan2x=sec2x=1/cos2x1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x=1/\cos^2x; all divisions are valid because the original domain already has cosx≠0\cos x\ne0. Multiply the original inequality by 2>02>0, and substitute: 2sinxcosx+tanx≥2,2y1+y2+y−2≥0,2y+y(1+y2)−2(1+y2)1+y2≥0.\begin{aligned} 2\sin x\cos x+\tan x&\ge2,\\ \frac{2y}{1+y^2}+y-2&\ge0,\\ \frac{2y+y(1+y^2)-2(1+y^2)}{1+y^2}&\ge0. \end{aligned} The denominator 1+y21+y^2 is strictly positive for every real yy. Multiplication by it therefore preserves the inequality: 2y+y+y3−2−2y2≥0,y3−2y2+3y−2≥0,(y−1)(y2−y+2)≥0.\begin{aligned} 2y+y+y^3-2-2y^2&\ge0,\\ y^3-2y^2+3y-2&\ge0,\\ (y-1)(y^2-y+2)&\ge0. \end{aligned} Complete the square in the quadratic factor: y2−y+2=(y−12)2+74>0.y^2-y+2=\left(y-\frac12\right)^2+\frac74>0. By the factor-sign method, the sign of the product is exactly the sign of y−1y-1. Consequently the inequality is equivalent to y≥1y\ge1, or tanx≥1\tan x\ge1.

On each branch (−π/2+nπ,π/2+nπ)(-\pi/2+n\pi,\pi/2+n\pi), tangent is increasing and takes the value 11 at x=π/4+nπx=\pi/4+n\pi. Hence x∈⋃n∈ℤ[nπ+π4,nπ+π2).\boxed{x\in\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} \left[n\pi+\frac\pi4,\,n\pi+\frac\pi2\right).} At the left endpoint the original left side is 1/2+(1/2)⋅1=11/2+(1/2)\cdot1=1, so it is included. The right endpoint is an asymptote and is excluded even though the inequality is non-strict.

Checking the algebra. The linear terms 2y2y and yy combine to give 3y3y. Expanding the factorisation provides a useful check: (y−1)(y2−y+2)=y3−y2+2y−y2+y−2=y3−2y2+3y−2.(y-1)(y^2-y+2) =y^3-y^2+2y-y^2+y-2 =y^3-2y^2+3y-2.

Example 5.9

Half-angle tangents and the equality case

Let A,B,C>0A,B,C>0 with A+B+C=πA+B+C=\pi. Prove tan2A2+tan2B2+tan2C2≥1,\tan^2\frac A2+\tan^2\frac B2+\tan^2\frac C2\ge1, and determine precisely when the inequality is strict.

Solution.

Each half-angle lies in (0,π/2)(0,\pi/2), so its tangent exists and is positive. Put u=tanA2,v=tanB2,w=tanC2.u=\tan\frac A2,\qquad v=\tan\frac B2,\qquad w=\tan\frac C2. We first establish the relation uv+vw+wu=1uv+vw+wu=1, rather than quoting it. Since (A+B+C)/2=π/2(A+B+C)/2=\pi/2, the cosine of this sum is zero. Expanding the cosine addition formula twice gives 0=cosA2cosB2cosC2−sinA2sinB2cosC2−sinA2cosB2sinC2−cosA2sinB2sinC2.\begin{aligned} 0={}&\cos\frac A2\cos\frac B2\cos\frac C2 -\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\cos\frac C2\\ &-\sin\frac A2\cos\frac B2\sin\frac C2 -\cos\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2. \end{aligned} Divide by the positive product cos(A/2)cos(B/2)cos(C/2)\cos(A/2)\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2). Term by term, this becomes 0=1−uv−uw−vw,souv+vw+wu=1.0=1-uv-uw-vw, \qquad\text{so}\qquad uv+vw+wu=1. Now use a sum of squares: u2+v2+w2−1=u2+v2+w2−(uv+vw+wu)=12((u−v)2+(v−w)2+(w−u)2)≥0.\begin{aligned} u^2+v^2+w^2-1 &=u^2+v^2+w^2-(uv+vw+wu)\\ &=\frac12\bigl((u-v)^2+(v-w)^2+(w-u)^2\bigr)\\ &\ge0. \end{aligned} This proves the required non-strict inequality. Equality holds exactly when all three squares vanish, that is, when u=v=wu=v=w. Tangent is strictly increasing on (0,π/2)(0,\pi/2), so equal half-angle tangents imply A/2=B/2=C/2A/2=B/2=C/2. The sum condition then gives A=B=C=π/3A=B=C=\pi/3. Conversely, at those angles each squared tangent is tan2(π/6)=1/3\tan^2(\pi/6)=1/3, and the sum is 11. tan2A2+tan2B2+tan2C2≥1,strictly greater than 1 iff the triangle is not equilateral.\boxed{\tan^2\frac A2+\tan^2\frac B2+\tan^2\frac C2\ge1,} \qquad \boxed{\text{strictly greater than \(1\) iff the triangle is not equilateral}.} The distinction between ≥\ge and >>. The equilateral triangle attains the value 11, so the bound for all triangles uses ≥\ge. The strict inequality >1>1 holds precisely when the angles are not all equal. Positivity also places all three half-angles on the same branch, where tangent is defined and strictly increasing.

What is the weakest domain condition for the nonstrict result? Positivity is convenient, but is not necessary for the inequality with ≥\ge. The same proof works for arbitrary real A+B+C=πA+B+C=\pi, provided none of the half-angle tangents is undefined. Equivalently, none of A,B,CA,B,C is an odd multiple of π\pi. The cosine product is then nonzero. Dividing the expanded equation by it is valid even if the product is negative. Thus uv+vw+wu=1uv+vw+wu=1 and the sum-of-squares argument still apply. Equality in this more general setting means u=v=wu=v=w; it need not mean that the three real angles themselves are equal.

5.4 Solving equations graphically: pictures, comparisons and root counts

An equation f(x)=g(x)f(x)=g(x) asks for inputs at which two outputs agree. On a common set of axes, the corresponding points have the same horizontal coordinate xx and the same vertical coordinate yy. They are therefore intersection points of the two graphs. The solutions are their xx-coordinates, not the points themselves and not their yy-coordinates.

This interpretation is useful, but a small drawing is not a proof that we have found all the intersections. A crossing might be far outside the window, two crossings might be very close, or an open endpoint might not be part of the graph. The examples below develop a reliable habit: domain→search interval→sketch→crossings and the number of roots.\text{domain}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{search interval} \ \longrightarrow\ \text{sketch}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{crossings and the number of roots}. We shall distinguish exact algebraic comparisons from the graphical shape information used with them. A formal justification of the latter is marked for a return visit after Calculus.

All angles in this section use the radian measure. Changing the angle unit changes equations such as sinx=x/10\sin x=x/10.

Tools for reading and checking a graph

Reading a crossing in a familiar graph. Recall the trigonometric graphs and the exponential and logarithmic graphs. Within one of the unbroken pieces already drawn in those sections, imagine following the curve with a pencil. If it starts below a horizontal line and finishes above that line, the pencil has to pass through the line somewhere in between. The picture says at least one crossing; it does not say that there is only one.

For two curves, compare their heights at the same input. Their height difference is H(x)=f(x)−g(x)H(x)=f(x)-g(x). A negative value means that the first curve lies below the second; a positive value means that it lies above. When their familiar unbroken shapes exchange these positions, we read a crossing between the two inputs. The signs locate a crossing even when a small drawing cannot show its exact position.

A word about the justification. This is an intuitive reading of the graph families we have already studied. We are not yet proving a theorem about all functions. In the next Calculus module, the relevant idea is called continuity, and the theorem that makes this crossing argument precise is the intermediate value theorem. Their names are given only for a future connection; you do not need their definitions here. A return discussion is in Further Study after Calculus. Do not use the pencil picture to jump across a missing input, a tangent asymptote or a step of the floor function. Check the domain first.

Monotonicity and uniqueness. If one graph strictly rises while the other falls, they can meet at most once. Here is the reason using the two-input definition of monotonicity. If a<ba<b, an increasing first function has f(a)<f(b)f(a)<f(b), while a decreasing second function has g(a)>g(b)g(a)>g(b). If the two functions already agree at aa, then f(b)>f(a)=g(a)>g(b),f(b)>f(a)=g(a)>g(b), so they cannot agree again at bb. More generally, a strictly increasing or strictly decreasing difference H=f−gH=f-g can equal zero at most once. Thus the crossing picture supplies existence, and an output comparison can supply uniqueness. These are two different jobs.

Reading an arch and its chords

Recall the geometric meaning of concavity. A chord is the straight segment joining two points of a curve. For the downward-bending arches below, the curve lies above this segment at every input strictly between its endpoints. This is the shape we shall use; the word arch by itself is not enough to guarantee it.

Why does this shape help us count intersections with a straight line? Suppose that there were three intersection points, from left to right A,B,CA,B,C. The segment ACAC would lie on the line. But the curve's chord shape would put BB strictly above that segment, whereas an intersection must be on it. Both cannot happen. Consequently, a curve with this chord shape can meet a straight line at most twice.

In the sine and logarithm examples, we shall use the familiar shape of the curve as a graphical input. The midpoint calculations below help us understand why the shape is reasonable: they compare the curve and its chord exactly at the middle input. Repeating that calculation checks the quarter points, the eighth points, and so on. This is not yet a proof for every real input. The step from those subdivision points to all inputs uses an idea from Calculus, explained later in the full midpoint-to-chord argument. For the present reading, keep the picture and the midpoint calculation together, and keep track of where this graphical shape is being used.

Why a positive sine arch has this shape

Look first at the sine arch in the figure below, and compare it with the sine graph from Lecture 2. Choose two inputs 0≤a<b≤π0\le a<b\le\pi, and put m=(a+b)/2m=(a+b)/2. The curve's height above this middle input is sinm\sin m. The chord's height there is the average (sina+sinb)/2(\sin a+\sin b)/2, because a straight segment has the average height at its midpoint.

The sine addition formulas give the exact comparison sina+sinb2=sinmcos(b−a2)<sinm.\frac{\sin a+\sin b}{2} =\sin m\cos\left(\frac{b-a}{2}\right)<\sin m. Indeed, 0<m<π0<m<\pi, so sinm>0\sin m>0, while 0<(b−a)/2≤π/20<(b-a)/2\le\pi/2, so its cosine is strictly less than one. Multiplying the positive number sinm\sin m by that cosine makes it smaller. Thus the curve really is above its chord at the midpoint; this feature is not a drawing error.

The same calculation works on either half of the interval, and then on either half of those halves. It explains the repeated midpoint pattern in the picture. We shall read the whole familiar sine arch as lying above its chords. As explained in the chord discussion, this full shape is a graphical input here; its all-point justification is left to the later Calculus discussion.

By periodicity, the same shape repeats after a shift by an integer multiple of 2π2\pi. Replacing xx by kxkx, with k>0k>0, changes the horizontal scale but leaves the order and relative positions of the points unchanged. Thus the positive arches of sin(kx)\sin(kx) have the same chord shape. We will compare each such arch directly with a straight line.

Why a logarithmic curve lies above its chords

Recall the shape of the increasing logarithm in Lecture 2. Its curve bends above a chord joining two graph points. Here too we can check the midpoint exactly. For distinct positive numbers a,ba,b, the square (a−b)2(\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2 is positive. Expanding gives a+b−2ab>0,soa+b2>ab.a+b-2\sqrt{ab}>0, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \frac{a+b}{2}>\sqrt{ab}. By monotonicity, applying the increasing function ln\ln preserves the inequality. The logarithm laws give ln(a+b2)>lnab=lna+lnb2.\ln\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right) >\ln\sqrt{ab}=\frac{\ln a+\ln b}{2}. The left side is the curve's midpoint height; the right side is the chord's midpoint height. This exact calculation explains the logarithmic curve's bending in the same way as the sine identity explains the sine arch. The comparison can again be repeated at quarter points and eighth points. For the present graphical argument, we use the familiar whole-curve shape; the step covering every input belongs to the return discussion after Calculus.

Multiplying every height by a positive number preserves which height is larger. In particular, the graph y=4lnxy=4\ln x has the same above-chord shape. The three-intersection argument then says that it can meet a straight line at most twice.

Why tangent rises faster than the line of slope one

First recall the unit-circle picture used for the trigonometric functions. We need a geometric comparison, which we derive here. For 0<t<π/20<t<\pi/2, the sector of angle tt has area t/2t/2, whereas the triangle formed by the positive horizontal radius, the tangent to the circle at the endpoint of that radius, and the ray of angle tt has area tant/2\tan t/2. The sector lies strictly inside the triangle apart from its boundary. Therefore tant>t(0<t<π/2).\tan t>t\qquad(0<t<\pi/2). By the radian sector-area formula, the sector occupies the fraction t/(2π)t/(2\pi) of the unit disk, whose area is π\pi. Hence its area is π⋅t/(2π)=t/2\pi\cdot t/(2\pi)=t/2. The triangle has base 11 and height tant\tan t, so its area is tant/2\tan t/2. These are ordinary area formulas. The sector formula uses radians, which is another reason the angle unit matters here.

Now let 0≤p<q<π/20\le p<q<\pi/2. The tangent subtraction identity gives tanq−tanp=tan(q−p)(1+tanptanq)≥tan(q−p)>q−p.\tan q-\tan p =\tan(q-p)\bigl(1+\tan p\tan q\bigr) \ge\tan(q-p)>q-p. For two negative inputs in (−π/2,0](-\pi/2,0], apply this same result to −q<−p-q<-p and use the oddness identity tan(−u)=−tanu\tan(-u)=-\tan u. For inputs on opposite sides of zero, add the two comparisons from each input to zero. Consequently, for any −π/2<p<q<π/2-\pi/2<p<q<\pi/2, (tanq−q)−(tanp−p)>0.(\tan q-q)-(\tan p-p)>0. Thus tanx−x\tan x-x is strictly increasing on the central tangent branch. On any other branch, subtract the same integer multiple of π\pi from both inputs. By tangent's period π\pi, its values repeat, and the difference between the inputs is unchanged. The conclusion therefore holds separately on every branch. It does not compare points separated by an asymptote.

What a numerical answer can and cannot do. A calculator can help us locate a crossing, but displaying a few decimal values cannot tell us that there is no other crossing. We count by combining exact sign calculations, algebraic restrictions, comparisons of outputs and the stated shape of the familiar graphs. In the diagrams, decimal coordinates are used only to place dots. The optional section Further Study after Calculus adds formal existence and shape arguments to these graphical explanations.

Locating a crossing more closely by interval halving

Suppose we have identified a single crossing between aa and bb, with opposite signs of the height difference H=f−gH=f-g at the endpoints. To narrow down its position, evaluate HH at the midpoint m=(a+b)/2m=(a+b)/2. If H(m)=0H(m)=0, we have found the root. Otherwise retain the half whose endpoint signs are opposite: its picture still starts on one side of the horizontal axis and ends on the other. This is the crossing picture on a smaller interval.

Each step halves the width. Starting with width b−ab-a, the successive widths are b−a2,b−a4,b−a8,…\frac{b-a}{2},\quad \frac{b-a}{4},\quad \frac{b-a}{8},\quad\ldots After a specified number nn of steps, the width is (b−a)/2n(b-a)/2^n. Any point inside that retained interval is at most its width from the root; its midpoint is at most half the width from the root. This is a numerical procedure using only substitution and sign comparisons. We make a finite number of steps to obtain the requested accuracy; no new limiting process is needed for that calculation. The formal theorem ensuring that each retained interval contains a crossing is discussed after the Calculus module.

When using decimal computations, keep enough digits to make the signs reliable. A displayed zero produced by rounding does not establish an exact root.

Example 5.10

A sine curve and a shallow line

Find the number of real solutions of sinx=x/10\sin x=x/10.

Solution.

Step 1: restrict the search before drawing. Use the range restriction from the sine graph: every sine value lies in [−1,1][-1,1], so a solution must satisfy −1≤x10≤1,hence−10≤x≤10.-1\le\frac{x}{10}\le1, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad -10\le x\le10. Put H(x)=sinx−x/10H(x)=\sin x-x/10. Both terms are odd, so HH is odd. Therefore H(0)=0H(0)=0, and every positive root has one negative partner. We need only count the positive roots carefully.

Step 2: count on the first positive sine arch, [0,π][0,\pi]. Use the familiar above-chord shape explained in the sine-arch picture. By the three-intersection argument, the arch can meet the line at most twice, including any endpoint intersection. Also, H(0)=0,H(π/2)=1−π20>0,H(π)=−π10<0.H(0)=0,\qquad H(\pi/2)=1-\frac{\pi}{20}>0,\qquad H(\pi)=-\frac{\pi}{10}<0. At the middle input the sine curve is above the line; at the right endpoint it is below. The crossing picture therefore places an intersection in (π/2,π)(\pi/2,\pi). There cannot be two positive intersections on this arch, because together with the one at 00 they would give three intersections with the same line. Thus the graphical count on this arch is exactly one positive root.

Step 3: discard the negative arch. For π≤x≤2π\pi\le x\le2\pi, sine is nonpositive but x/10>0x/10>0. Equality is impossible, including both endpoints.

Step 4: count on [2π,3π][2\pi,3\pi]. By periodicity, this is another arch of the same shape. The exact height comparisons are H(2π)=−π5<0,H(5π/2)=1−π4>0,H(3π)=−3π10<0.H(2\pi)=-\frac{\pi}{5}<0,\qquad H(5\pi/2)=1-\frac{\pi}{4}>0,\qquad H(3\pi)=-\frac{3\pi}{10}<0. The middle value is positive because π<4\pi<4. The curve is below the line at both ends and above it in the middle. The crossing picture gives one intersection on each side of 5π/25\pi/2, and the chord shape permits at most two. Thus this arch contributes exactly two positive roots.

Step 5: check the last piece and use symmetry. Since 3π<10<4π3\pi<10<4\pi, sine is nonpositive on [3π,10][3\pi,10], whereas x/10x/10 is positive. There are no more positive roots. We have found three positive roots, their three negative partners, and zero: 3+3+1=7 real solutions.\boxed{3+3+1=7\text{ real solutions}.} Their approximate positive locations are 2.85234,7.06817,8.423202.85234,7.06817,8.42320. This count uses the familiar unbroken sine arch and its above-chord shape. Their formal justification, followed by a slope-based treatment of both sine examples, is given in the optional Calculus discussion.

Example 5.11

Locating the first tangent intersection

Show that the least positive solution of tanx=x+1\tan x=x+1 lies in (π/4,π/2)(\pi/4,\pi/2). How many real solutions are there altogether?

Solution.

Begin with the common domain. The tangent graph excludes its asymptotes x=π/2+kπx=\pi/2+k\pi, k∈ℤk\in\mathbb Z.

Set H(x)=tanx−x−1H(x)=\tan x-x-1. On each tangent branch Ik=(kπ−π/2,kπ+π/2),I_k=(k\pi-\pi/2,k\pi+\pi/2), we use one unbroken branch of the tangent graph. For any two inputs a<ba<b on that branch, the geometric tangent comparison gives H(b)−H(a)=(tanb−tana)−(b−a)>0.H(b)-H(a)=(\tan b-\tan a)-(b-a)>0. Thus HH is strictly increasing on the whole branch: tangent gains more height than the line gains between any two inputs. As the input approaches the left end of this branch, tangent falls without bound; as it approaches the right end, tangent rises without bound. The line x+1x+1 stays bounded near each finite endpoint, so HH is negative sufficiently near the left end and positive sufficiently near the right end. The crossing picture therefore gives a root on this branch; the output comparison proves that there is at most one. This reasoning applies to each branch separately, so the graphical count is exactly one on every branch, hence infinitely many real roots.

On the central branch, calculate rather than estimate from the picture: H(0)=−1<0,H(π/4)=1−π/4−1=−π/4<0,H(0)=-1<0,\qquad H(\pi/4)=1-\pi/4-1=-\pi/4<0, whereas H(x)H(x) becomes arbitrarily large as xx approaches π/2\pi/2 from the left. The unique central root is therefore in (π/4,π/2)(\pi/4,\pi/2). All branches to its left contain only negative inputs, and all branches to its right start at π/2\pi/2 or later. It is the least positive root. Numerically it is about 1.132271.13227, but the requested conclusion is the exact enclosure π/4<xmin<π/2.\boxed{\pi/4<x_{\min}<\pi/2.} Neither endpoint is a solution: the first fails substitution, and the second is outside the domain. A second proof of the increase on each branch appears in the optional Calculus discussion.

Example 5.12

Incompatible signs

Find the number of real solutions of sinx=x2+x+1\sin x=x^2+x+1.

Solution.

Use a nonnegative square to bound the quadratic and locate the parabola's lowest point: x2+x+1=(x+12)2+34≥34.x^2+x+1=\left(x+\frac12\right)^2+\frac34\ge\frac34. This alone does not prove there is no solution: sine can also take values between 3/43/4 and 11. We must compare the outputs at the same input. Since sinx≤1\sin x\le1, a solution would require x2+x+1≤1⇔x(x+1)≤0⇔−1≤x≤0.x^2+x+1\le1 \iff x(x+1)\le0 \iff -1\le x\le0. For these inputs, −π<x≤0-\pi<x\le0, so the sine graph gives sinx≤0\sin x\le0. But the quadratic is at least 3/4>03/4>0. Equality is impossible. Outside this interval the quadratic exceeds 11, so equality is also impossible there. Therefore There are no real solutions.\boxed{\text{There are no real solutions.}} This proof explains the separation seen in the drawing; it does not infer separation just because the two curves happen to look apart.

Example 5.13

Exponential growth and a fourth power

Find the number of real solutions of ex=x4e^x=x^4.

Solution.

The graphical count is three real solutions: one negative and two positive. We shall use the exponential and logarithmic graphs, exact algebraic comparisons and the stated logarithmic chord shape. The two crossings near the origin and the more distant positive crossing require different viewing scales. We therefore identify the intervals of the crossings and explain the count before relying on a single viewing window.

At x=0x=0, the two sides are 11 and 00, so zero is not a root. For every other real xx, both sides are positive, and the logarithm laws from Appendix A give the equivalent equation ex=x4⇔x=ln(x4)=4ln|x|.e^x=x^4 \iff x=\ln(x^4)=4\ln|x|. The absolute value is essential: lnx\ln x is not real for negative xx, whereas ln(x4)\ln(x^4) is defined there.

Negative inputs: exactly one root. Write x=−tx=-t, where t>0t>0. The equation becomes e−t=t4.e^{-t}=t^4. By monotonicity, as tt increases the left side strictly decreases and the right side strictly increases. They can therefore agree at most once. At t=0t=0, these two formulas have values 11 and 00; at t=1t=1, their values are e−1<1e^{-1}<1 and 11. Their relative heights have reversed. Reading the familiar unbroken graphs as in the crossing picture gives one crossing with 0<t<10<t<1, hence one root with −1<x<0-1<x<0.

Positive inputs: exactly two roots. The same positive intersections can be counted by drawing y=4lnxy=4\ln x and y=xy=x. Use the familiar logarithmic chord shape explained by the positive-square midpoint calculation. By the three-intersection argument, this curve can meet the line at most twice on the entire positive axis. The full chord shape is the graphical input in this part of the solution.

To show that both intersections actually occur, we need values on opposite sides of the line. Use the bounds 2<e<32<e<3 for the exponential base, and put K(x)=4lnx−xK(x)=4\ln x-x. The logarithm laws give K(x)=ln(x4ex),K(x)=\ln\left(\frac{x^4}{e^x}\right), so K(x)K(x) is positive precisely when x4>exx^4>e^x, and negative precisely when x4<exx^4<e^x. The following comparisons need only integer powers: K(1)=−1<0,e2<32=9<16=24⇒K(2)>0,e4<34=81<256=44⇒K(4)>0,e16>216=164⇒K(16)<0.\begin{aligned} K(1)&=-1<0,\\ e^2&<3^2=9<16=2^4 &&\Longrightarrow K(2)>0,\\ e^4&<3^4=81<256=4^4 &&\Longrightarrow K(4)>0,\\ e^{16}&>2^{16}=16^4 &&\Longrightarrow K(16)<0. \end{aligned} The curve is below the line at 11, above it at 22 and 44, and below it again at 1616. The crossing picture gives one intersection in (1,2)(1,2) and another in (4,16)(4,16). These intervals do not overlap, so the intersections are distinct. The chord argument allows at most two positive intersections altogether; there can be no additional one near zero, between these intervals, or beyond 1616. Combining the negative and positive cases, 1+2=3 real solutions.\boxed{1+2=3\text{ real solutions}.} Their approximate locations are −0.81555,1.42961,8.61317-0.81555,1.42961,8.61317. These decimal values explain why a short horizontal window can give the wrong count. After the Calculus module, return to the formal justification of the graphical shape and compare this solution with the slope and area method.

Example 5.14

A logarithmic curve and two diagonals

Find the number of real solutions of log10x=x\log_{10}x=x.

Solution.

The domain rule for the logarithm gives x>0x>0. We compare the logarithmic curve with the increasing line y=xy=x, and show that the curve lies below the line for every admissible input.

Step 1: the interval 0<x≤10<x\le1. Here log10x≤0\log_{10}x\le0, while x>0x>0. The two sides cannot agree.

Step 2: inputs x>1x>1. Choose the positive integer nn with n≤x<n+1n\le x<n+1. For example, if 3≤x<43\le x<4, take n=3n=3. We will use the elementary inequality 10n≥n+1(n=1,2,3,…).10^n\ge n+1\qquad(n=1,2,3,\ldots). It holds at n=1n=1, since 10≥210\ge2. If it holds for an integer n≥1n\ge1, then 10n+1=10⋅10n≥10(n+1)>n+2,10^{n+1}=10\cdot10^n\ge10(n+1)>n+2, so it holds at the next integer as well. Starting with n=1n=1, this step establishes n=2n=2; repeating it establishes n=3n=3, and so on. Any chosen positive integer is reached after finitely many repetitions. This familiar chain of implications is called mathematical induction.

Consequently x<n+1≤10nx<n+1\le10^n. Apply the increasing logarithm of base 1010, and then use the logarithm laws, to obtain log10x<log10(10n)=n≤x.\log_{10}x<\log_{10}(10^n)=n\le x. The first inequality is strict even when xx is itself an integer, because x<n+1x<n+1 is still strict. Hence the logarithmic curve lies strictly below the diagonal throughout this interval. Thus equality is impossible in this interval too, and log10x=x has 0 real solutions.\boxed{\log_{10}x=x\text{ has }0\text{ real solutions}.}

Changing the sign of the diagonal. Now consider the related equation log10x=−x\log_{10}x=-x. The function L(x)=log10x+xL(x)=\log_{10}x+x is strictly increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty), because both summands are strictly increasing by the output-comparison rule. Since L(1/10)=−9/10<0<L(1)=1L(1/10)=-9/10<0<L(1)=1, the familiar unbroken logarithmic curve exchanges sides with the line between those inputs. The crossing picture, together with monotonicity, gives exactly one root, approximately 0.399010.39901. Replacing y=xy=x by y=−xy=-x changes the number of intersections from zero to one. The inequality-based Calculus approach is developed separately in the optional discussion.

Example 5.15

Two very close crossings

Find the number of real solutions of sin(πx/2)=99x/500\sin(\pi x/2)=99x/500.

Solution.

Step 1: range restriction and symmetry. The sine range forces every solution to satisfy |99x500|≤1,so|x|≤R:=50099.\left|\frac{99x}{500}\right|\le1, \qquad\text{so}\qquad |x|\le R:=\frac{500}{99}. Here 5<R<65<R<6. The difference H(x)=sin(πx/2)−99x/500H(x)=\sin(\pi x/2)-99x/500 is odd, so zero is a root and nonzero roots occur in opposite pairs.

Step 2: the first positive arch. The scaled sine arch on [0,2][0,2] has the same above-chord shape as the first arch in the earlier sine example. Here H(0)=0,H(1)=1−99500=401500>0,H(2)=−198500<0.H(0)=0,\qquad H(1)=1-\frac{99}{500}=\frac{401}{500}>0, \qquad H(2)=-\frac{198}{500}<0. The same crossing and chord-shape argument used in the first sine example gives exactly one positive root in (1,2)(1,2). On [2,4][2,4], sine is nonpositive and the line is positive, so there are no roots.

Step 3: the second positive arch. The crucial comparison is not approximate: H(4)=−396500<0,H(5)=1−495500=1100>0.H(4)=-\frac{396}{500}<0,\qquad H(5)=1-\frac{495}{500}=\frac1{100}>0. At the right endpoint of the permissible search interval, the line has height one. Because 5<R<65<R<6, the angle πR/2\pi R/2 lies strictly between 5π/25\pi/2 and 3π3\pi, where sine is strictly less than one. Therefore H(R)=sin(πR/2)−1<0.H(R)=\sin(\pi R/2)-1<0. The crossing picture gives one root in (4,5)(4,5) and another in (5,R)(5,R). By periodicity, the arch on [4,6][4,6] has the same chord shape as the first one. The three-intersection argument permits at most two intersections on that arch, so these are its only two roots. In particular, no extra root can be hidden in the short interval near the top of the arch.

Thus there are exactly three positive roots, three negative roots and zero: 7 real solutions.\boxed{7\text{ real solutions}.} The positive roots are approximately 1.77181,4.79774,5.040361.77181,4.79774,5.04036. The final two crossings are close because at the peak x=5x=5, the line lies only 0.010.01 below the sine curve.

Example 5.16

The fixed point of cosine

Find the number of real solutions of cosx=x\cos x=x.

Solution.

The cosine range is [−1,1][-1,1], so every root lies in that interval. For −1≤x<0-1\le x<0, cosine is positive, since [−1,0)⊂(−π/2,0)[-1,0)\subset(-\pi/2,0), while xx is negative. At x=0x=0, the outputs are 11 and 00. Thus all possible roots lie in (0,1](0,1].

On [0,1][0,1], use the monotonicity comparison: cosx\cos x is strictly decreasing and xx is strictly increasing. They can therefore agree at most once. To spell out the comparison, if a<ba<b were two roots, we would have a=cosa>cosb=ba=\cos a>\cos b=b, contradicting a<ba<b. To locate a crossing in the familiar cosine graph, compare the exact heights using H(x)=cosx−xH(x)=\cos x-x: H(0)=1>0,H(1)=cos1−1<0.H(0)=1>0,\qquad H(1)=\cos1-1<0. The last inequality is strict because 11 radian is not a multiple of 2π2\pi. The curve is above the line at 00 and below it at 11. The crossing picture places a root in (0,1)(0,1), and the monotonicity argument makes it unique: Exactly one real solution, approximately 0.73909.\boxed{\text{Exactly one real solution, approximately }0.73909.} The line y=xy=x is useful here because an intersection with it means that the output equals the input: such an input is called a fixed point.

Floor and fractional part: intersections with endpoint rules

Recall the floor and fractional-part definitions: n=⌊x⌋∈ℤ,t={x}=x−⌊x⌋∈[0,1),x=n+t.n=\lfloor x\rfloor\in\mathbb Z,\qquad t=\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\in[0,1),\qquad x=n+t. The floor is the greatest integer not exceeding the input; fractional part is the nonnegative remainder after that integer is removed. For instance, −1.3=−2+0.7-1.3=-2+0.7, so ⌊−1.3⌋=−2\lfloor-1.3\rfloor=-2 and {−1.3}=0.7\{-1.3\}=0.7. It is not correct to truncate negative inputs towards zero.

On the strip [n,n+1)[n,n+1), the floor graph is the horizontal segment y=ny=n, with a closed left endpoint and an open right endpoint. The fractional-part graph is the rising segment y=x−ny=x-n, also closed on the left and open on the right. These endpoint conventions are part of the function, not optional decoration. The decomposition x=n+tx=n+t turns a sketch into an exact proof.

Example 5.17

Can an integer equal a fractional part?

Solve ⌊x⌋={x}\lfloor x\rfloor=\{x\} over the real numbers.

Solution.

Write n=⌊x⌋n=\lfloor x\rfloor and t={x}t=\{x\}. The equation is n=tn=t, where nn is an integer and 0≤t<10\le t<1. The only integer in [0,1)[0,1) is zero. Hence n=0n=0, then t=0t=0, and finally x=n+t=0.x=n+t=0. Conversely, ⌊0⌋=0={0}\lfloor0\rfloor=0=\{0\}, so the candidate really works. Thus x=0is the unique solution.\boxed{x=0\quad\text{is the unique solution}.} Why is x=1x=1 not another answer? At that input the floor has jumped to 11, but the fractional part has reset to 00. An open dot approaching height 11 from the left does not give the value at the endpoint.

Example 5.18

A line meets two floor steps

Solve 4{x}=x+⌊x⌋4\{x\}=x+\lfloor x\rfloor over the real numbers.

Solution.

First express the equation as an intersection of familiar curves. Using {x}=x−⌊x⌋\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor, 4{x}=x+⌊x⌋⇔4(x−⌊x⌋)=x+⌊x⌋⇔4x−4⌊x⌋=x+⌊x⌋⇔3x=5⌊x⌋⇔⌊x⌋=35x.\begin{aligned} 4\{x\}=x+\lfloor x\rfloor &\iff4(x-\lfloor x\rfloor)=x+\lfloor x\rfloor\\ &\iff4x-4\lfloor x\rfloor=x+\lfloor x\rfloor\\ &\iff3x=5\lfloor x\rfloor\\ &\iff\lfloor x\rfloor=\frac35x. \end{aligned} Every step is reversible, so this graph intersection problem has exactly the same solutions as the original equation.

Now prove exactly which floor steps can be met. Put x=n+tx=n+t, with n∈ℤn\in\mathbb Z and 0≤t<10\le t<1. The original equation becomes 4t=(n+t)+n=2n+t⇔3t=2n⇔t=2n3.4t=(n+t)+n=2n+t \iff3t=2n \iff t=\frac{2n}{3}. The condition that this is a fractional part gives 0≤2n3<1⇔0≤n<32.0\le\frac{2n}{3}<1 \iff0\le n<\frac32. As nn must be an integer, only n=0n=0 and n=1n=1 are possible. For n=0n=0, we get t=0t=0 and x=0x=0. For n=1n=1, we get t=2/3t=2/3 and x=5/3x=5/3.

Check both in the original equation. Zero gives 0=00=0. At 5/35/3, ⌊5/3⌋=1\lfloor5/3\rfloor=1 and {5/3}=2/3\{5/3\}=2/3, giving 4⋅23=83=53+1.4\cdot\frac23=\frac83=\frac53+1. Therefore x∈{0,53}.\boxed{x\in\left\{0,\frac53\right\}.} The integer restriction explains why a line that continues indefinitely meets only these two steps: the strip-consistency condition rules out every other integer height.

Example 5.19

An inequality with a jump boundary

Solve ⌊x⌋−1+x2≥0\lfloor x\rfloor-1+x^2\ge0 over the real numbers.

Solution.

Rearrange without changing the inequality direction: x2+⌊x⌋−1≥0⇔x2−1≥−⌊x⌋.x^2+\lfloor x\rfloor-1\ge0 \iff x^2-1\ge-\lfloor x\rfloor. Thus we compare the parabola y=x2−1y=x^2-1 with the descending staircase y=−⌊x⌋y=-\lfloor x\rfloor, selecting inputs where the parabola is on or above the staircase. We consider the integer strips separately, checking the value at every boundary where a formula changes.

Case 1: x≥1x\ge1. Then ⌊x⌋≥1\lfloor x\rfloor\ge1, so x2+⌊x⌋−1≥x2≥1>0.x^2+\lfloor x\rfloor-1\ge x^2\ge1>0. Every such input works, including x=1x=1.

Case 2: 0≤x<10\le x<1. Here ⌊x⌋=0\lfloor x\rfloor=0, and the expression is x2−1<0x^2-1<0. No input in this strip works.

Case 3: −1≤x<0-1\le x<0. Here ⌊x⌋=−1\lfloor x\rfloor=-1, and the expression is x2−2≤−1<0x^2-2\le-1<0. Again there is no solution. At x=0x=0, Case 2 already gives the value −1-1.

Case 4: −2≤x<−1-2\le x<-1. Here ⌊x⌋=−2\lfloor x\rfloor=-2, so we need x2−3≥0⇔x≤−3orx≥3.x^2-3\ge0 \iff x\le-\sqrt3\ \text{or}\ x\ge\sqrt3. Intersect with the current strip. The positive alternative is irrelevant, and we obtain [−2,−3][-2,-\sqrt3]. The endpoint −3-\sqrt3 belongs because equality is allowed and its floor really is −2-2.

Case 5: every remaining negative strip, x<−2x<-2. It is not enough to check only the few steps visible in the graph. The floor inequality ⌊x⌋>x−1\lfloor x\rfloor>x-1 holds for every real xx, because x−⌊x⌋<1x-\lfloor x\rfloor<1. Therefore, for x≤−2x\le-2, x2+⌊x⌋−1>x2+x−2=(x+2)(x−1)≥0.x^2+\lfloor x\rfloor-1 >x^2+x-2=(x+2)(x-1)\ge0. The product is nonnegative because both factors are nonpositive there. This single estimate covers all the infinitely many strips to the left.

Combine the accepted pieces: (−∞,−3]∪[1,∞).\boxed{(-\infty,-\sqrt3]\ \cup\ [1,\infty).}

Why the two boundary points have different meanings. At x=−3x=-\sqrt3, the curves genuinely intersect: x2−1=2=−⌊x⌋x^2-1=2=-\lfloor x\rfloor. At x=1x=1, however, x2−1=0,−⌊x⌋=−1.x^2-1=0,\qquad-\lfloor x\rfloor=-1. They do not intersect there. The inequality becomes true because the staircase jumps down at 11. The step immediately to the left has height zero, but the endpoint at (1,0)(1,0) is open for that step. The closed point is (1,−1)(1,-1). This is why a solution interval for an inequality involving a jump may begin at a point where the equation of its two sides is false.

What these ten examples teach us

The method is not simply “draw two curves and count.” The sine examples use the sine range, symmetry, exact height comparisons and the arch picture. The tangent example treats each branch separately. The exponential example warns that a valid local sketch may omit a distant crossing. The logarithmic example warns that the wrong sign on a line changes the problem. The floor examples require integer strip conditions and careful open and closed endpoints. In each case the picture organizes the reasoning. We distinguish the algebraic steps from any graphical crossing idea whose formal justification belongs to the Calculus module.

5.5 Chords of the sine curve and inequalities between slopes

We next compare the slopes of lines joining the origin to points on the sine curve. Here a slope means the ordinary rise divided by run of a straight line, as in coordinate geometry; it is not the derivative of a curve. Why should one of these lines be steeper than another? We shall read the picture using heights at the same input, then carry out the resulting algebra one step at a time.

Why the sine curve lies above its chords

Look at the first quarter of the sine graph. It rises from O=(0,0)O=(0,0) towards (π/2,1)(\pi/2,1), becoming flatter as it rises. Choose Q=(b,sinb)Q=(b,\sin b), with 0<b≤π/20<b\le\pi/2, and draw the straight segment OQOQ. The familiar sine arch sits above this segment between its endpoints. The diagrams in the next two examples show precisely the curve and segments we are comparing.

To translate the picture into an inequality, choose an input tt with 0<t<b0<t<b. The line OQOQ rises sinb\sin b units over a horizontal run of bb units, so its slope is sinb/b\sin b/b. Starting from the origin, its height after travelling tt units horizontally is tsinb/bt\sin b/b. The sine curve's height at that same input is sint\sin t. Thus the above-the-chord picture says sint>tbsinb(0<t<b≤π2).\sin t>\frac tb\sin b\qquad\left(0<t<b\le\frac\pi2\right). This is a graphical explanation of the comparison. A drawing alone does not establish it at every real input: that complete argument is in the later-reading section, where continuity is available. For now, concentrate on how the heights in the picture become the two sides of the inequality.

Dividing both sides by t>0t>0 gives sintt>sinbb.\frac{\sin t}{t}>\frac{\sin b}{b}. The ray from OO to (t,sint)(t,\sin t) is therefore steeper than OQOQ. Taking positive reciprocals reverses the inequality; this follows from multiplying an inequality by the positive product of its denominators, as in the inequality rules.

Example 5.20

If 0<A<π/60<A<\pi/6, prove AcscA<π/3A\csc A<\pi/3.

Solution.

Since 0<A<π/60<A<\pi/6, both AA and sinA\sin A are positive. In particular, cscA=1/sinA\csc A=1/\sin A exists. Solution.

Reading the slopes. Every interior ray in the sine-curve picture has slope greater than the endpoint ray from (0,0)(0,0) to (π/2,1)(\pi/2,1).
