5.6 Choosing a Graphical Method

The first step is to recognise the feature that controls the problem: a period, an equality case, an algebraic factor, a change in monotonicity, or a jump. The following comparisons collect the main ideas of the lecture. Use the links to return to their explanations whenever a similar feature appears in a new problem.

Guiding ideaHow it determines the answer
PeriodicityTranslate a tangent solution interval by every nπn\pi. Translations by 2nπ2n\pi alone omit alternate branches.
Angle restrictionsFor triangle angles, cosA+cosB+cosC=3/2\cos A+\cos B+\cos C=3/2 exactly in the equilateral case. Distinct unrestricted real angles can still give equality.
Algebraic reductiony3−2y2+3y−2=(y−1)(y2−y+2)y^3-2y^2+3y-2=(y-1)(y^2-y+2). The quadratic factor is positive, so the sign depends only on y−1y-1.
Equality casesThe sum of the three squared half-angle tangents is at least 11; it is greater than 11 precisely for a non-equilateral triangle.
Viewing scaleex=x4e^x=x^4 has one negative and two positive roots. The larger positive intersection lies well beyond the two crossings near the origin.
Comparing diagonalslog10x=x\log_{10}x=x has no real root, whereas log10x=−x\log_{10}x=-x has exactly one.
Jump endpointsFor x2+⌊x⌋−1≥0x^2+\lfloor x\rfloor-1\ge0, the endpoint x=1x=1 is included even though the two comparison curves do not meet there.
Chord slopesA smaller positive angle gives a steeper chord from the origin on the sine curve. Taking positive reciprocals reverses the slope inequality.
Inverse branchesA quadratic has two maximal one-to-one intervals. On each restriction, choose its range as the codomain before defining the inverse.

💡 Five questions to ask before declaring a solution complete

  1. Have I used the original domain, including every pole and hole?

  2. Have I found all possible intervals, not just the portion in the sketch?

  3. Which step reads a familiar graph, and which steps follow from algebra?

  4. Have I checked strictness, equality and jump endpoints separately?

  5. Can I explain why each transformation or algebraic step is reversible?

In Lecture 6 we will bring these methods together with graphical transformations to solve problems involving several function families.

5.7 Further Study after Calculus

§ When to read this section

This section is not required on a first reading. Return to it after completing the Calculus module. We now justify the crossing and chord pictures used in the main lecture. Continuity explains the crossing argument and the passage from subdivision points to an entire chord. Derivatives then provide further methods for graph shape, turning points and numerical refinement.

Why the graphical crossing and chord arguments work

This subsection is for a return visit after the Calculus module. On a first reading, the familiar unbroken curves and arch shapes guide our pictures. Here we explain the additional theorem behind that reasoning. The algebraic sign calculations in the examples remain the same.

Continuity and the intermediate value theorem. In Calculus, continuity gives a precise meaning to the idea that the output has no sudden jump at an input. The intermediate value theorem says: if HH is continuous on the whole closed interval [a,b][a,b], and H(a)<0<H(b)H(a)<0<H(b), then there is an input cc with a<c<ba<c<b and H(c)=0H(c)=0. The same conclusion holds when the two signs are reversed. Applied to H=f−gH=f-g, this theorem justifies the crossing picture used earlier. The conclusion is at least one crossing. A separate argument is needed to rule out a second crossing.

The familiar sine and cosine functions are continuous everywhere; exponential and logarithmic functions are continuous on their domains; and tangent is continuous within each one of its branches. Differences of continuous functions are continuous. Thus the theorem applies on all the closed intervals used in the preceding examples. It does not apply across a tangent asymptote or across a jump of the floor function. Those points must be treated by the domain and endpoint rules already used in the main lecture.

The same theorem explains why interval halving retains a root in the half whose endpoint signs differ. Repeated halving makes the enclosing interval as short as desired. The earlier numerical error bound follows simply from that interval's length.

An arch cannot cross a line three times

Recall the geometric meaning of concavity. A function FF is strictly concave on an interval if its graph lies strictly above every chord joining two distinct points of the graph. Precisely, for a<ba<b and 0<t<10<t<1, the input x=(1−t)a+tbx=(1-t)a+tb lies between aa and bb, and the chord has height (1−t)F(a)+tF(b)(1-t)F(a)+tF(b) there. Strict concavity means F((1−t)a+tb)>(1−t)F(a)+tF(b).F((1-t)a+tb)>(1-t)F(a)+tF(b). The word chord means a straight segment joining two points of the curve. It does not mean a tangent line.

Suppose that a strictly concave graph met a straight line at three inputs a<b<ca<b<c. The segment joining the first and third intersections would be part of that line. At the middle input bb, strict concavity would put the curve strictly above this segment, contradicting the middle intersection. Thus a strictly concave graph meets any straight line at most twice. Equivalently, subtracting a line from a strictly concave function gives a strictly concave function with at most two zeros.

The midpoint calculations in the main lecture provide the algebraic part. Continuity supplies the remaining step. For a continuous function, it is enough to establish the midpoint comparison F(a+b2)≥F(a)+F(b)2(a<b).F\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)\ge\frac{F(a)+F(b)}2 \qquad(a<b). Here is why this one comparison controls an entire chord.

First bisect. Fix the endpoints a,ba,b, and let ℓ(x)\ell(x) be the line through their graph points. At the endpoints F=ℓF=\ell. The midpoint inequality gives F≥ℓF\ge\ell at the midpoint as well, because a line's midpoint height is the average of its endpoint heights.

Then bisect again. Apply the same inequality on each half. The values at the quarter points are at least the averages of the adjacent already established values, and these averages are at least the corresponding heights on ℓ\ell. Repeating this reasoning proves F≥ℓF\ge\ell at every input of the form a+k2n(b−a),0≤k≤2n.a+\frac{k}{2^n}(b-a),\qquad 0\le k\le2^n. These are simply the points obtained by repeatedly halving the interval. Given any other input between aa and bb, these subdivision points can be chosen arbitrarily close to it. Continuity carries the inequality to that input. Therefore the whole graph lies on or above the chord.

Finally obtain strictness. Suppose that the midpoint inequality is strict whenever its two inputs differ. Put G(x)=F(x)−ℓ(x)G(x)=F(x)-\ell(x). We have just proved G≥0G\ge0 on [a,b][a,b]. For an interior input xx, choose δ>0\delta>0 small enough that x−δ,x+δ∈[a,b]x-\delta,x+\delta\in[a,b]. The strict midpoint inequality, after subtracting the line's midpoint identity, gives G(x)>G(x−δ)+G(x+δ)2≥0.G(x)>\frac{G(x-\delta)+G(x+\delta)}2\ge0. Hence the graph is strictly above the chord at every interior input, not only at the repeated subdivision points.

For the sine graph, the strict midpoint inequality follows from the addition formula. For the logarithmic graph, it follows from a positive square and the logarithm laws. Both functions are continuous on the intervals in question, so the argument above now turns those midpoint calculations into full chord inequalities. This is the extra justification that was deliberately left for a return visit after Calculus.

The sine chord: the complete all-point argument

The first-reading discussion compares heights in a picture. We now justify that comparison at every real input. This argument uses the continuity and limit ideas from the Calculus module.

For 0≤u<v≤π/20\le u<v\le\pi/2, the sine addition formula gives sinu+sinv2=sinu+v2cosv−u2<sinu+v2.\frac{\sin u+\sin v}{2} =\sin\frac{u+v}{2}\cos\frac{v-u}{2} <\sin\frac{u+v}{2}. The strict sign is justified as follows. The midpoint angle (u+v)/2(u+v)/2 is positive, so its sine is positive. Also 0<(v−u)/2≤π/40<(v-u)/2\le\pi/4, so the cosine factor lies strictly between 00 and 11. Multiplying a positive number by a number less than 11 makes it smaller. The displayed inequality says that the curve's height at the midpoint is strictly above the midpoint height of the chord.

From midpoints to every point on a chord. Fix b∈(0,π/2]b\in(0,\pi/2] and join (0,0)(0,0) to (b,sinb)(b,\sin b). At b/2b/2, the midpoint inequality places sine above the chord. Apply the same midpoint argument on [0,b/2][0,b/2] and [b/2,b][b/2,b]: the curve is at least as high as the original chord at b/4b/4 and 3b/43b/4. Repeating gives, for every integer n≥0n\ge0 and 0≤k≤2n0\le k\le2^n, sin(k2nb)≥k2nsinb.\sin\left(\frac{k}{2^n}b\right) \ge\frac{k}{2^n}\sin b. The induction works because the chord is a straight line: its midpoint height is exactly the average of its endpoint heights. These repeatedly halved subdivisions get arbitrarily close to every point in [0,b][0,b]. Sine and the straight line are continuous, so passing to such an approximating sequence gives sint≥tbsinb(0≤t≤b).\sin t\ge\frac tb\sin b\qquad(0\le t\le b). Here continuity means that inputs approaching tt have sine values approaching sint\sin t; the inequality is preserved in that limit.

We can also justify strictness at every interior point, not just at the subdivision points. If 0<t≤b/20<t\le b/2, the strict midpoint inequality on [0,2t][0,2t], followed by the non-strict result at 2t2t, gives sint>sin0+sin(2t)2≥12(0+2tbsinb)=tbsinb.\sin t>\frac{\sin0+\sin(2t)}2 \ge\frac12\left(0+\frac{2t}{b}\sin b\right) =\frac tb\sin b. If b/2<t<bb/2<t<b, apply it instead on [2t−b,b][2t-b,b]: sint>sin(2t−b)+sinb2≥12(2t−bbsinb+sinb)=tbsinb.\sin t>\frac{\sin(2t-b)+\sin b}{2} \ge\frac12\left(\frac{2t-b}{b}\sin b+\sin b\right) =\frac tb\sin b. Thus in both cases we have proved the strict chord inequality sint>tbsinb(0<t<b≤π2).\boxed{\sin t>\frac tb\sin b \qquad\left(0<t<b\le\frac\pi2\right).} Dividing by t>0t>0 gives the equivalent slope comparison sintt>sinbb.\boxed{\frac{\sin t}{t}>\frac{\sin b}{b}.} This is the exact statement expressed by the earlier chord diagrams. It is a special case of the sine-arch chord comparison used in the intersection problems; the argument above spells it out for chords through the origin. A derivative proof appears below. The argument uses trigonometric identities together with continuity; the passage from subdivision points to every real input is the additional Calculus step.

Slopes, monotonicity and curvature

The derivative H′(x)H'(x) is the instantaneous slope of a graph. Where the limit exists, its definition is H′(x)=limh→0H(x+h)−H(x)h.H'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{H(x+h)-H(x)}h. The quotient before taking the limit is the slope of the line joining (x,H(x))(x,H(x)) and (x+h,H(x+h))(x+h,H(x+h)). The limiting value describes the slope of the tangent at the first point.

The mean value theorem connects such local slopes with the change over an interval. If HH is continuous on [a,b][a,b] and differentiable on (a,b)(a,b), then some c∈(a,b)c\in(a,b) satisfies H(b)−H(a)=H′(c)(b−a).H(b)-H(a)=H'(c)(b-a). Since b−a>0b-a>0, a positive derivative throughout an interval makes the function strictly increasing there; a negative derivative makes it strictly decreasing. A nonnegative derivative gives a nondecreasing function, which need not be strictly increasing without a further argument. We shall make that distinction explicitly in the tangent example.

The formulas needed below are (sinx)′=cosx,(cosx)′=−sinx,(tanx)′=sec2x,(lnx)′=1x(x>0).(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad (\cos x)'=-\sin x,\qquad (\tan x)'=\sec^2x,\qquad (\ln x)'=\frac1x\quad(x>0). The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives; a constant factor remains a constant factor; and (cx)′=c(cx)'=c. The chain rule gives (sin(kx))′=kcos(kx)(\sin(kx))'=k\cos(kx). Applying differentiation twice produces the second derivative. In particular, (sin(kx))″=−k2sin(kx),(lnx)″=−1x2.(\sin(kx))''=-k^2\sin(kx),\qquad (\ln x)''=-\frac1{x^2}. The derivative of the logarithm is developed from area in Appendix B's calculus foundation; more applications are collected in its monotonicity section.

Why a negative second derivative proves strict concavity. If F″<0F''<0, then F′F' is strictly decreasing. For three inputs a<b<ca<b<c, apply the mean value theorem separately on [a,b][a,b] and [b,c][b,c]. There are points u∈(a,b)u\in(a,b) and v∈(b,c)v\in(b,c) with F(b)−F(a)b−a=F′(u)>F′(v)=F(c)−F(b)c−b.\frac{F(b)-F(a)}{b-a}=F'(u)>F'(v) =\frac{F(c)-F(b)}{c-b}. Multiply by the positive product (b−a)(c−b)(b-a)(c-b), collect the two terms containing F(b)F(b), and divide by c−ac-a. This gives F(b)>c−bc−aF(a)+b−ac−aF(c).F(b)>\frac{c-b}{c-a}F(a)+\frac{b-a}{c-a}F(c). The expression on the right is exactly the height at input bb of the chord joining the first and third graph points. Thus the graph lies strictly above that chord. If the second derivative is positive instead, the inequalities reverse, and the graph lies strictly below the chord: it is strictly convex. A straight line has zero second derivative, so adding or subtracting a line does not change either curvature test.

The sine intersections revisited

Return to the equation sinx=x/10\sin x=x/10. For H(x)=sinx−x/10H(x)=\sin x-x/10, differentiation gives H′(x)=cosx−110,H″(x)=−sinx.H'(x)=\cos x-\frac1{10},\qquad H''(x)=-\sin x. On the interior of each positive sine arch, H″<0H''<0, so HH is strictly concave. This supplies a Calculus proof of the shape used earlier. On the first arch [0,π][0,\pi], the three values H(0)=0,H(π/2)=1−π/20>0,H(π)=−π/10<0H(0)=0,\qquad H(\pi/2)=1-\pi/20>0, \qquad H(\pi)=-\pi/10<0 produce one positive zero; two positive zeros would join the zero at the origin to contradict strict concavity. On [2π,3π][2\pi,3\pi], the values at the left endpoint, peak and right endpoint have signs −,+,−-,+,-, so there are exactly two zeros. The negative arches contribute none for positive inputs; odd symmetry adds three negative roots to the three positive roots and zero. The count is again seven.

For the equation with two close crossings, put H(x)=sin(πx/2)−99x/500H(x)=\sin(\pi x/2)-99x/500. Then H″(x)=−π24sin(πx/2).H''(x)=-\frac{\pi^2}{4}\sin(\pi x/2). It is negative on the positive arches (0,2)(0,2) and (4,6)(4,6). The exact sign tests in the elementary proof therefore combine with this curvature test to give one positive root on the first arch and two on the second. The small positive value H(5)=1/100H(5)=1/100 remains essential: curvature alone does not say whether a line passes below, through or above the top region of an arch.

One intersection on each tangent branch

For the equation tanx=x+1\tan x=x+1, put H(x)=tanx−x−1H(x)=\tan x-x-1. On each branch Ik=(kπ−π/2,kπ+π/2)I_k=(k\pi-\pi/2,k\pi+\pi/2), H′(x)=sec2x−1=tan2x≥0.H'(x)=\sec^2x-1=\tan^2x\ge0. The derivative vanishes only at the isolated point x=kπx=k\pi on that branch. The mean value theorem first tells us that HH is nondecreasing. To obtain strict increase, choose any a<ba<b in the branch. Inside (a,b)(a,b), choose a smaller closed interval [u,v][u,v] which avoids kπk\pi. On this smaller interval the derivative is positive, so H(u)<H(v)H(u)<H(v). Nondecrease on the whole branch now gives H(a)≤H(u)<H(v)≤H(b).H(a)\le H(u)<H(v)\le H(b). Thus H(a)<H(b)H(a)<H(b), as required. Merely writing H′≥0H'\ge0 and asserting strict increase would have omitted this justification.

Moreover, limx→(kπ−π/2)+H(x)=−∞,limx→(kπ+π/2)−H(x)=+∞.\lim_{x\to(k\pi-\pi/2)^+}H(x)=-\infty, \qquad \lim_{x\to(k\pi+\pi/2)^-}H(x)=+\infty. Continuity and strict increase give exactly one root on every branch. On the central branch, H(0)=−1H(0)=-1 and H(π/4)=−π/4H(\pi/4)=-\pi/4 are negative, whereas H(x)→+∞H(x)\to+\infty at the right asymptote. Therefore its root is in (π/4,π/2)(\pi/4,\pi/2), and it is the least positive root. Compare this argument with the sector-area and tangent-identity proof, which reaches the same conclusion without differentiation.

Exponential and polynomial growth: a slope-and-area proof

For the positive roots of ex=x4e^x=x^4, taking logarithms gives K(x)=4lnx−x=0K(x)=4\ln x-x=0, with x>0x>0. Now K′(x)=4x−1=4−xx.K'(x)=\frac4x-1=\frac{4-x}{x}. Since x>0x>0, its sign is positive for 0<x<40<x<4, zero at 44, and negative for x>4x>4. Hence the graph rises strictly up to x=4x=4 and falls strictly afterwards. This also locates the exact turning point, which was not needed in the elementary chord argument.

The area definition of the natural logarithm provides precise estimates without a decimal value: ln2=∫12dtt.\ln2=\int_1^2\frac{dt}{t}. For 1<t<21<t<2, the height 1/t1/t lies strictly between 1/21/2 and 11. The region under the curve on [1,2][1,2] therefore has area strictly between the areas of two rectangles of width one and heights 1/21/2 and 11: 12<ln2<1.\frac12<\ln2<1. The inequalities are strict because the curve differs from each rectangle's top edge throughout the interior. See the area construction in Appendix B.

Consequently, K(1)=−1<0,K(2)=4ln2−2>0.K(1)=-1<0,\qquad K(2)=4\ln2-2>0. Continuity and strict increase give exactly one root in (1,2)(1,2), and strict increase excludes any further root in (0,4](0,4]. Also K(4)>K(2)>0,K(16)=4ln16−16=16ln2−16<0.K(4)>K(2)>0,\qquad K(16)=4\ln16-16=16\ln2-16<0. Continuity and strict decrease give exactly one root in (4,16)(4,16), with no further root after 1616. Together with the unique negative root already proved by comparing the decreasing curve e−te^{-t} and the increasing curve t4t^4, this gives three real roots in all.

Keeping a logarithm below a diagonal

Return to the comparison of log10x\log_{10}x and xx. A useful general inequality is lnx≤x−1(x>0),\ln x\le x-1\qquad(x>0), with equality only at x=1x=1. To prove it using slopes, define J(x)=x−1−lnxJ(x)=x-1-\ln x. Then J′(x)=1−1x=x−1x.J'(x)=1-\frac1x=\frac{x-1}{x}. It is negative for 0<x<10<x<1 and positive for x>1x>1. Thus JJ decreases towards J(1)=0J(1)=0, and increases away from that point. Its minimum is zero, proving the inequality. Geometrically, y=x−1y=x-1 is the tangent to y=lnxy=\ln x at (1,0)(1,0), and this tangent lies above the curve.

The area estimate just proved gives ln2>1/2\ln2>1/2, so ln10>ln4=2ln2>1.\ln10>\ln4=2\ln2>1. For x>1x>1, the numerator lnx\ln x is positive; dividing it by the larger-than-one number ln10\ln10 strictly reduces it. Therefore log10x=lnxln10<lnx≤x−1<x.\log_{10}x=\frac{\ln x}{\ln10}<\ln x\le x-1<x. For 0<x≤10<x\le1, the logarithm is nonpositive and x>0x>0. Hence the two graphs never meet, agreeing with the elementary proof.

Refining a root with tangent lines

Interval halving already gives arbitrarily small enclosures without derivatives. Once derivatives are available, a tangent line can often predict a much closer input in one step. Starting at an input xnx_n with H′(xn)≠0H'(x_n)\ne0, the tangent to y=H(x)y=H(x) has equation y=H(xn)+H′(xn)(x−xn).y=H(x_n)+H'(x_n)(x-x_n). Set its height equal to zero and solve for its intersection with the horizontal axis: xn+1=xn−H(xn)H′(xn).x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{H(x_n)}{H'(x_n)}. This is Newton's method. It uses the zero of the tangent line as a new estimate for the zero of the curve. The estimate is not automatically exact, and a poor starting point can make the method fail. Retain a proven sign-changing interval and check the new estimate against it; interval halving remains available whenever a tangent step is unsuitable.

For the unique root of cosx=x\cos x=x, take H(x)=cosx−xH(x)=\cos x-x, so H′(x)=−sinx−1H'(x)=-\sin x-1. The iteration becomes xn+1=xn+cosxn−xn1+sinxn.x_{n+1}=x_n+\frac{\cos x_n-x_n}{1+\sin x_n}. Starting at x0=3/4x_0=3/4 gives, to the displayed precision, x1≈0.7391111388,x2≈0.7390851334.x_1\approx0.7391111388,\qquad x_2\approx0.7390851334. These decimals refine the location of the root whose location was first understood from the graph and whose existence and uniqueness are justified by the tools of this later-reading section. Numerical refinement and a proof that all roots have been found answer different questions; neither should be substituted for the other.

The sine-chord comparison revisited

Return to the two inequalities in the sine-chord section. Their first-reading explanation compares the sine curve with straight segments. After studying derivatives, the same comparisons can be obtained by showing that the chord slope R(x)=sinxx,0<x≤π2,R(x)=\frac{\sin x}{x},\qquad 0<x\le\frac\pi2, strictly decreases. The quotient rule gives R′(x)=xcosx−sinxx2.R'(x)=\frac{x\cos x-\sin x}{x^2}. The denominator is positive, so the question is the sign of the numerator. Define Q(x)=sinx−xcosxQ(x)=\sin x-x\cos x, now also allowing x=0x=0. The product rule gives Q′(x)=cosx−(cosx−xsinx)=xsinx>0(0<x≤π2).Q'(x)=\cos x-(\cos x-x\sin x)=x\sin x>0 \qquad\left(0<x\le\frac\pi2\right). Since Q(0)=0Q(0)=0, the mean value theorem implies Q(x)>0Q(x)>0 for every positive input in this interval. Therefore R′(x)=−Q(x)/x2<0R'(x)=-Q(x)/x^2<0. If 0<t<b≤π/20<t<b\le\pi/2, it follows that sintt>sinbb.\frac{\sin t}{t}>\frac{\sin b}{b}. Taking b=π/6b=\pi/6 gives sinA/A>3/π\sin A/A>3/\pi, hence AcscA<π/3A\csc A<\pi/3, for 0<A<π/60<A<\pi/6. Taking b=π/2b=\pi/2 gives t/sint<π/2t/\sin t<\pi/2. Apply that last bound to A,B,CA,B,C separately and add to obtain the second inequality. In both cases the endpoint restrictions and the reversal on taking positive reciprocals are the same as in the elementary proof.

The two later proofs justify the same geometry: the continuity argument extends midpoint comparisons to a whole chord, while the derivative argument measures how the chord slopes change. For the inverse-tangent chord, see the optional calculation following the graphical discussion in Day 5, Solution 6.
